newsitem.title: USA: Dow drops nearly 100 points; dollar, bonds rise.
newsitem.headline: Dow drops nearly 100 points; dollar, bonds rise.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks dropped nearly 100 points Thursday in hectic trading as the market was hit by a second consecutive day of heavy losses.
The dollar rose against most currencies, and bonds edged higher. Oil prices rebounded after this week's steep declines.

The Dow Jones industrial average ended down 98.81 points, or 1.54 percent, at 6,303.71 after giving back an early gain of 35 points. It was the Dow's biggest point loss since mid-July and followed a 71-point drop on Wednesday.
In the broader market, declining issues beat advances 1,616 to 877 on active volume of 492 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

"Investors were whipsawed," said Philip Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management. "They were emboldened at the opening from two fabulous economic reports and then a wave of computer-driven sell orders took the market hostage. Trading is still nervous."
In a turbulent session, the NYSE imposed trading curbs twice as the 30-stock Dow index fell 50 points in mid-afternoon, recovered somewhat and then plummeted again in late trading.

"It has become clearly evident that we have already seen the high for the Dow for the short-term," said Richard Cripps, chief market strategist of Legg Mason Wood Walker. "There is a loss of momentum in the stock market."

The mood of investors soured last Friday after Chairman Alan Greenspan that rattled markets around the world with a warning about "irrational exuberance" in financial markets. The comment was viewed as a hint that the central bank might resort to higher interest rates to slow the markets' ascent.
On Friday, the Dow tumbled nearly 145 points before recovering to end 82 points lower.

Stocks steadied on Monday and Tuesday but the market was shaken anew Wednesday by jitters about corporate earnings and speculation that Japanese investors might be losing their appetite for U.S. Treasury securities.
The dollar rose against most currencies amid optimism that negotiations in Dublin over a proposed European monetary pact would end in favour of the U.S. currency.
The dollar closed at 1.5410 German marks, compared with 1.5379 at Wednesday's close. Against the Japanese yen, the dollar rose to 113.15 yen vs. 112.97 at Wednesday's close.

The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond edged up 2/32 point, or 62.5 cents per $1,000 face value. Its yield, which moves in the opposite direction from the price, slipped to 6.62 percent from 6.63 percent Wednesday and compared with 6.49 percent on Tuesday.
Bonds were buoyed by a report that November retail sales fell 0.4 percent, suggesting that the economy was slowing as expected and inflation was still not a threat.
In other economic news, the Consumer Price Index for November rose an expected 0.3 percent. That followed benign inflation data in Wednesday's November wholesale price report.
Oil prices rebounded from this week's steep declines, as an outage at a East Coast refinery threatened to pinch supplies of gasoline in the Northeast.

January gasoline rose 1.16 cents to 64.72 cents a gallon at the New York Mercantile Exchange. January crude oil added 34 cents to $23.72 a barrel after falling more than $2 earlier this week. January heating oil rose 1.85 cents to 68.67 cents a gallon.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 stock index closed 8.2 points higher at 3,990.7. In Tokyo, the Nikkei 225 index closed at 20,501.20, down 67.18 points or 0.33 percent.
